             COMMENTS OF THE TEXAS ADVANCED ENERGY BUSINESS ALLIANCE
                                  ON THE PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION


INTRODUCTION



         The Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance (“TAEBA”) appreciates the opportunity

to comment on proposed new 16 Texas Administrative Code §25.521 concerning the Large

Load Demand Management Service (“LLDMS”).



         TAEBA is a statewide business association representing companies engaged in the

development and deployment of advanced energy technologies and services in Texas,

including distributed energy resources, energy storage, microgrids, demand response, solar

generation, energy efficiency, and other technologies that improve the reliability, affordability,

and resilience of the Texas electric system.



         TAEBA reaffirms its April 8, 2026 recommendations that the Commission: (1)

incorporate LLDMS into ERS; (2) in conjunction with that integration, either remove the ERS

budget cap or increase it to $150 million; (3) permit participation by loads that respond to four

coincident peak or a successor transmission-cost allocation methodology; and (4) establish

deployment triggers that consider actual system conditions in addition to extreme weather.




Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance                                 P.O. Box 301151, Austin, TX 78703
                                                                                TexasAdvancedEnergy.org
        These comments address an additional implementation issue: whether participating

large load customers may use on-site backup generation, or bring-your-own generation

(BYOG), when ERCOT initiates LLDMS activities before an Energy Emergency Alert (EEA) has

been declared.



COMMENTS ON PROPOSED §25.521(d), (e), AND (f): CLARIFICATION REGARDING ON-SITE

BACKUP GENERATION



       TAEBA previously supported participation by large loads providing demand reductions

through BYOG because that generation would be deployed specifically to support the grid in

response to an ERCOT instruction.



       PURA §37.0561(e) expressly provides that its requirements regarding on-site backup

generation do not prohibit a large load customer from participating in a service authorized by

PURA §39.170(b). It also specifies that ERCOT’s authority does not authorize or require a

violation of applicable emissions limitations or other environmental regulations.



       The proposed rule, however, creates uncertainty regarding when such generation may

be operated. Proposed §25.521(d) would allow ERCOT to procure LLDMS based on monthly

modeling, weekly forecasts, or in advance of an anticipated EEA Level 1. Proposed §25.521(e)

appears to authorize deployment during an actual EEA, while proposed §25.521(f)

contemplates availability verification during the LLDMS obligation period.



       Together, these provisions do not clearly establish whether a participating customer

could be required to physically demonstrate availability, reduce its demand, or operate on-site

generation before an EEA has officially been declared.



       This distinction is important because some on-site backup generators may operate

under TCEQ authorizations that limit when and how they may be used. For example, 30 TAC


                                                              Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance   2
 §106.511 applies to generators used only for portable, emergency, or standby services. It is

unclear whether operation during an anticipated or pre-EEA LLDMS event would be

permissible under these authorizations.



       Federal Power Act (FPA) §202(c) provides a potential, but event-specific, mechanism for

addressing these constraints. In January 2026, at ERCOT’s request, the U.S. Department of

Energy (DOE) issued an amended §202(c) order authorizing ERCOT to direct certain customer-

owned backup generators to operate after ERCOT had deployed all available market services,

except frequency-responsive services, and before or during EEA Level 3, even if operation

would exceed applicable federal environmental permit limits. A separate §202(c) order for

generation resources recited ERCOT’s representation that TCEQ would exercise enforcement

discretion for generators exceeding state emissions requirements during the same winter-

weather event. Both orders were time-limited and subject to specific conditions. (See DOE

Amended Order No. 202-26-01A and Order No. 202-26-04, Jan. 25, 2026.)



       ERCOT has since discussed the development of FPA §202(c) requests with

stakeholders. (See ERCOT, April 27, 2026 WMWG Agenda, Item 4.) The LLDMS framework

should therefore explain whether and how ERCOT would seek, structure, and implement a

§202(c) order for participating large loads that rely on BYOG, including the relationship

between any such order, LLDMS deployment, and EEA timing. Because §202(c) relief is event-

specific and does not automatically resolve all TCEQ requirements, participants also need

advance clarity regarding notice, the resources and operating periods covered, and

compliance treatment when no applicable federal order or state relief is in effect.



       TAEBA respectfully recommends that the Commission:



       1. Clarify whether ERCOT may physically deploy LLDMS, or require physical operation

           to verify availability, before an EEA is declared;




                                                                Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance   3
        2. If pre-EEA operation is contemplated, coordinate with TCEQ and obtain clear

          guidance regarding the circumstances under which a participating customer may

          legally operate permitted on-site backup generation in response to an ERCOT

          instruction;

       3. Clarify how ERCOT will coordinate any FPA §202(c) request or order with LLDMS,

          including deployment sequencing, notice to covered customers, applicable

          operating conditions, and the treatment of participants when no federal order or

          state relief is in effect; and

       4. Ensure that ERCOT’s qualification, deployment, and compliance protocols account

          for applicable restrictions on backup-generator operation and do not place

          participating customers in conflict with their environmental requirements.



       TAEBA is not requesting that the Commission interpret or modify requirements

administered by TCEQ, nor does TAEBA assume that relief under FPA §202(c) will be available

for any particular LLDMS event. Rather, TAEBA requests coordination among the Commission,

ERCOT, TCEQ, and, where appropriate, DOE so that customers understand when BYOG may

be used and can evaluate LLDMS participation without risking regulatory noncompliance.



CONCLUSION



       Clear guidance regarding pre-emergency deployment, the use of on-site backup

generation, and the coordination of any FPA §202(c) authority would support TAEBA’s

previously stated goal of enabling BYOG resources to participate in LLDMS while ensuring

compliance with applicable requirements. TAEBA respectfully requests that the Commission

resolve these issues before ERCOT finalizes the program’s implementing protocols.




                                                            Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance   4
                      Respectfully submitted,

       EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE TEXAS ADVANCED ENERGY BUSINESS ALLIANCE


   The Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance provides the Commission with the following

recommendations:



   •    Clarify whether ERCOT may physically deploy LLDMS, or require physical operation to

        verify availability, before an Energy Emergency Alert is declared;

   •    If pre-emergency operation is contemplated, coordinate with TCEQ to clarify when

        participating customers may legally operate permitted on-site backup generation in

        response to an ERCOT instruction;

   •    Clarify how ERCOT will coordinate any FPA §202(c) request or order with LLDMS,

        including deployment sequencing, customer notice, applicable operating conditions,

        and treatment when no federal order or state relief is in effect;

   •    Ensure that ERCOT’s qualification, deployment, and compliance protocols account for

        applicable restrictions on backup-generator operation and do not place participating

        customers in conflict with environmental requirements;

   •    Incorporate LLDMS into the Emergency Response Service;

   •    In conjunction with that integration, either remove the ERS budget cap or increase it to

        $150 million;

   •    Permit participation by loads that respond to four coincident peak or a successor

        transmission-cost allocation methodology; and

   •    Establish deployment triggers that consider actual system conditions in addition to

        extreme weather.
